title: Issues Navigable Waters Protection Rule
description_short: EPA and the Army Corps issued the Navigable Waters Protection Rule, narrowing federal Clean Water Act protections.
description_medium: The Environmental Protection Agency and Army Corps issued the Navigable Waters Protection Rule on April 21, 2020. The rule narrowed which waters fell under federal Clean Water Act protections, changing the reach of federal permitting and pollution controls. Its supporters described it as clarifying jurisdiction; critics warned that fewer waterways would be protected.
description_long: On April 21, 2020, the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers issued the Navigable Waters Protection Rule, narrowing the federal definition of waters covered by the Clean Water Act. That change reduced the waterways subject to federal permitting and pollution controls, shifting more responsibility to state and local governments. The agencies said the rule clarified the statute’s reach; environmental groups warned that streams and wetlands left outside the definition would lose federal safeguards. The dispute mattered because the definition helped determine which projects required federal review and which pollution limits applied. A narrower scope could ease permitting for some landowners and developers while leaving more waterways to state law. The rule became a major point of conflict over federal authority and the balance between development and water protection.

description_short: Judge Arthur Engoron issued a gag order after Trump posted a disparaging comment about the judge’s law clerk.

description_long: On October 3, 2023, Judge Arthur Engoron barred Donald Trump from making public statements about court staff involved in New York’s civil-fraud trial. description_short: Trump repeatedly called press fake news and enemy of the people, escalating attacks on free press and journalism.

description_long: On February 26, 2026, The Guardian reported that the Justice Department had not released three FBI memos documenting four 2019 interviews with a woman who made unsubstantiated allegations that Donald Trump sexually abused her as a minor with Jeffrey Epstein’s assistance. The Guardian said it obtained and reviewed the missing reports, and an administration official confirmed they were authentic. The woman’s claims have not been corroborated; the FBI brought no charges related to them, and some details conflict with what is known about Epstein’s life in the early 1980s. Trump has denied wrongdoing. The department said the documents were duplicative or privileged, while Democrats on the House Oversight Committee demanded an accounting of why they were withheld. title: Phase One China Trade Deal Fails to Meet Targets — Agricultural Purchases Fall Short
description_short: Phase One China Trade Deal Fails to Meet Targets — Agricultural Purchases Fall Short
description_medium: The Phase One trade deal with China, signed with great fanfare on January 15, 2020, failed to meet its ambitious purchasing targets as China bought significantly less American agricultural and manufactured goods than promised. China's purchases fell far short of the $200 billion in additional purchases over two years that the deal had promised. The shortfall undermined Trump's claim that he had achieved a historic trade victory. The deal largely preserved the tariff structure while delivering minimal structural changes to Chinese trade practices.
description_long: The United States and China signed the Phase One trade agreement on January 15, 2020. China committed to purchase an additional $200 billion in U.S. goods and services over two years, including agricultural and manufactured products. A Peterson Institute for International Economics tracker found that China ultimately purchased about 58 percent of the goods and services covered by its commitment, with agricultural purchases also falling well below target. The shortfall weakened Donald Trump’s claim that the agreement had secured a major trade victory. The deal left many tariffs in place and did not deliver the structural changes to Chinese trade practices sought by the administration. The pandemic and trade conditions shaped the period, but the purchase gap remained central to assessing the agreement’s results. The Phase One deal produced a written commitment and continued negotiations, while its headline buying targets went unmet.

title: Trump Claims Absolute Presidential Immunity from Prosecution
description_short: Trump Claims Absolute Presidential Immunity from Prosecution
description_medium: In October 2023, Trump legal team made the unprecedented argument that a former president has absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for any official acts taken while in office. Judge Tanya Chutkan rejected the argument in the DC Jan 6 case, writing that presidents are not kings. Trump appealed to the DC Circuit and ultimately the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case and delayed the trial indefinitely. Legal scholars called the immunity claim the most sweeping assertion of executive power in American history.
description_long: In October 2023, Donald Trump’s lawyers argued that a former president had absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts taken while in office. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan rejected the claim in the federal January 6 case, and the D.C. Circuit affirmed that decision. The Supreme Court agreed to hear Trump’s appeal, delaying the trial while it considered the scope of presidential immunity. In 2024, the Court held that former presidents have absolute immunity for core constitutional powers, presumptive immunity for other official acts, and no immunity for unofficial acts. The ruling returned the case to lower courts to determine which allegations involved official conduct. The dispute raised a major constitutional question: how to protect executive decision-making without placing a former president beyond criminal law. The distinction between official and private actions became central to the prosecution and to future cases involving presidential conduct.

title: Trump Shares Classified Intel with Russian Officials in Oval Office

The episode intensified scrutiny of Trump’s handling of national-security information and the trust required for intelligence-sharing relationships. title: White House Restricts Press Briefing Access to Pro-Trump Outlets Only
description_short: White House Restricts Press Briefing Access to Pro-Trump Outlets Only
description_medium: The Trump White House restructured press briefing access in 2025 to prioritize and reserve front-row seating and guaranteed questioning rights for outlets deemed friendly, including right-wing and MAGA-aligned media, while systematically excluding or limiting access for traditional mainstream news organizations. The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the changes as destroying the nonpartisan press access standards that had governed White House journalism for decades.
description_long: In 2025, the White House changed how journalists received briefing-room seats and opportunities to ask questions, expanding access for conservative outlets and online personalities while traditional news organizations faced limits. The New York Times reported that Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt cultivated relationships with pro-Trump media figures. The White House Correspondents’ Association criticized the changes as a departure from nonpartisan access practices that had governed the briefing room for decades. Access to briefings matters because journalists use them to question officials and report the administration’s decisions to the public. The new approach gave the White House greater influence over who received prominent seating and guaranteed opportunities to ask questions. It also challenged the role of an independent press corps in setting access rules. The changes did not remove every established outlet from briefings, but they altered the balance between legacy news organizations and ideologically aligned media.

title: Trump Threatens to Sue CNN and NYT Over Iran Strike Intelligence Reporting
description_short: Trump Threatens to Sue CNN and NYT Over Iran Strike Intelligence Reporting

The NYT's lawyer responded that 'no retraction is needed' and 'no apology will be forthcoming.' Trump publicly called NYT and CNN reporters 'BAD PEOPLE WITH EVIL INTENTIONS' and 'sick.'
description_long: On June 26, 2025, Donald Trump’s personal attorney sent legal letters to CNN and the New York Times demanding retractions and threatening defamation suits over reporting on a Defense Intelligence Agency assessment of U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear sites. The reports said the strikes delayed Iran’s nuclear program by months, at odds with Trump’s public claim that the facilities had been “obliterated.” The Times’ lawyer rejected the demand, saying no retraction or apology would be forthcoming. Trump also attacked the outlets and their reporters publicly. The exchange brought pressure from the president’s lawyer to bear on reporting about classified intelligence and the administration’s account of the strikes. A demand letter is not a filed lawsuit, and neither outlet was found liable in the reported episode. The dispute raised questions about press freedom and the ability of news organizations to publish assessments that conflict with a president’s public statements.
